lines.text: From the tables, $P(z < \hl{1}{0.94}) = 0.8264$.

lines.text: Use $\hl{1}{z} = \dfrac{\hl{2}{x} - \hl{3}{\mu}}{\hl{4}{\sigma}}$ with $\hl{3}{\mu = 48.2}$ and $\hl{4}{\sigma = 10.6}$.

steps.ask: By symmetry, which area equals the chance of a weight greater than a z-score of −1.35?
steps.title: Find the probability of a greater weight

lines.text: By symmetry of the normal curve, $P(z > \hl{1}{-1.35}) = P(z < \hl{1}{1.35})$.

problems.note: This time two exams are compared, so each mark gets its own z-score and the two are compared. The formula is the same as before.

steps.ask: Use z = (x − μ)/σ for Maths first. Which numbers are x, μ and σ?
steps.title: Convert each mark to a z-score

lines.text: Use $\hl{1}{z} = \frac{\hl{2}{x} - \hl{3}{\mu}}{\hl{4}{\sigma}}$ to compare marks across exams.

steps.title: Do the same for English

steps.ask: Which z-score is larger, and what does a larger z-score say about Mary's result compared with the class?
steps.title: Compare the z-scores

lines.text: A higher z-score means Mary is further above the class average. $\hl{1}{-0.33}$ is bigger than $\hl{1}{-0.4}$.
So Mary did better in Maths, because her z-score there is higher (closer to the mean).
